q: Identify the type of the underlined noun in the sentence: "The *jury* was unanimous in its verdict."
e:
"Jury" refers to a group of people acting as a single unit, making it a Collective Noun.
When a collective noun acts as one unified body, it takes a singular verb ("was") and singular pronoun ("its").

q: Which of the following nouns is ALWAYS used in the singular form and does not take an '-s' plural in standard English?
e:
"Furniture" (like luggage, scenery, information, advice, and poetry) is an uncountable noun and has no plural form "furnitures".
To quantify it, we use phrases such as "pieces of furniture".

q: In the sentence "She *herself* painted the entire mural," the word "herself" functions as a/an:
e:
Placed immediately after the subject "She" solely to add emphasis (and removable without breaking grammar), "herself" is an Emphatic (Intensive) Pronoun.
A Reflexive Pronoun acts as the object of a verb or preposition (e.g., "She blamed herself").

q: Fill in the blank with the correct form: "Mount Everest is _____ than any other peak in the world."
e:
When comparing one item with "any other" member of the same class, the comparative degree ("higher") is used followed by "than".
"Highest" is used in the superlative without "than" (e.g., "the highest peak in the world").

q: Identify the nature of the verb in the sentence: "The birds *flew* swiftly across the sky."
e:
Here "flew" does not take a direct object ("across the sky" is a prepositional phrase of place), so it functions as an Intransitive Verb.
In "The boy flew a kite," the same verb becomes transitive because "a kite" is its direct object.

q: Choose the most appropriate modal auxiliary: "Candidates _____ bring their admit cards to the examination hall; entry is strictly barred without them."
e:
"Must" expresses strong obligation, necessity, or mandatory rule.
"Might", "could", and "may" indicate possibility or permission rather than strict compulsion.

q: Identify the kind of adverb italicized in the sentence: "He *seldom* misses his morning walk."
e:
"Seldom" answers the question "How often?", which defines an Adverb of Frequency (like always, often, rarely, never).
Adverbs of frequency normally precede the main verb and follow the verb "be".

q: Identify the part of speech of the italicized word: "Wait here *until* I return from the post office."
e:
"Until" joins the dependent adverbial clause "I return from the post office" to the main clause "Wait here", functioning as a Subordinating Conjunction.
When followed only by a noun phrase ("until Monday"), "until" acts as a preposition.

q: Which emotion is expressed by the interjection "Alas!" in the sentence "Alas! We have lost a noble teacher"?
e:
"Alas!" is a classic interjection expressing grief, sorrow, or pity.
"Hurrah!" expresses joy, "Bravo!" expresses applause, and "Hush!" calls for silence.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct article: "He is _____ university professor who holds _____ honorary doctorate."
e:
Article choice depends on initial SOUND, not spelling: "university" begins with a consonant /j/ ("yoo") sound → "a university"; "honorary" begins with a silent 'h' and vowel sound → "an honorary".
Other examples: "a European", "a one-rupee note", "an honest man", "an MLA".

q: Fill in the blank: "_____ Ganga is considered sacred by millions of people."
e:
The definite article "The" is always used before the names of rivers, seas, oceans, canals, and mountain ranges (e.g., the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Pacific).
However, single mountain peaks (Mount Everest) and lakes (Lake Superior) generally take no article.

q: Choose the correct option: "_____ gold is a precious metal, but _____ gold in this ring is impure."
e:
Material nouns used in a general sense take NO article ("Gold is a precious metal"), but when particularized or specified ("the gold in this ring"), they take "the".
The same rule applies to abstract nouns ("Honesty is the best policy" vs. "The honesty of the clerk").

q: Fill in the blank: "_____ of the two sisters has submitted her assignment on time."
e:
"Each" (or "Neither"/"Either") is used for two or more persons/things and takes a singular verb ("has") and singular pronoun ("her").
"Every" is only an adjective (never followed directly by "of"), while "All" and "Any" are not used with "of the two" in this singular construction.

q: What is the correct plural form of the foreign-origin noun "criterion"?
e:
Greek-origin nouns ending in "-on" form their plural by changing "-on" to "-a": criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena.
"Criterias" is a common grammatical error because "criteria" is already plural.

q: Identify the grammatical function of the italicized word: "*Swimming* is an excellent cardiovascular exercise."
e:
Here "Swimming" is a verbal noun acting as the subject of the verb "is", which makes it a Gerund.
A Present Participle functions as an adjective or forms continuous tenses (e.g., "The swimming child waved").

q: Identify the grammatical case of the italicized noun in: "Milton, the great *poet*, became blind in later life."
e:
"The great poet" stands next to the subject "Milton" to explain or rename it, so it is in the Nominative Case in Apposition.
A noun in apposition always takes the same case as the noun it explains.

q: Which of the following sentences uses the Possessive Case of compound/joint nouns CORRECTLY?
o: Ram's and Shyam's joint bakery is very famous.
Ram and Shyam's joint bakery is very famous.
My brother's-in-law house is near the station.
The table's leg was broken yesterday.
e:
For joint possession, the apostrophe (-'s) is added only to the LAST noun ("Ram and Shyam's joint bakery").
Option C should be "My brother-in-law's house", and Option D (inanimate object) should be "The leg of the table".

q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence regarding the order of personal pronouns:
o: I, you, and he will attend the seminar together.
He, you, and I will attend the seminar together.
You, he, and I will attend the seminar together.
I, he, and you have confessed our mistake.
e:
For positive/neutral singular statements, English follows the 2-3-1 rule: Second Person (You) + Third Person (he) + First Person (I).
For admitting a fault/guilt or plural pronouns, the 1-2-3 rule applies ("I, you, and he have confessed our mistake").

q: Fill in the blank with the most accurate relative pronoun: "All _____ glitters is not gold."
e:
After indefinite pronouns like "all, everything, nothing, only, same, little" and superlative adjectives, the relative pronoun "that" is preferred over "which" or "who".
Hence "All that glitters is not gold" is the standard idiomatic and grammatical form.

q: Spot the grammatically CORRECT sentence:
o: Let you and I solve this problem calmly.
Between you and I, the proposal seems flawed.
Let you and me solve this problem calmly.
He is taller than me am.
e:
Both the verb "let" and prepositions like "between" take the OBJECTIVE case ("me", "him", "us"), never the nominative ("I").
Thus "Let you and me..." and "Between you and me..." are correct.

q: Fill in the blank: "There is still _____ hope of his recovery, so the doctors have not given up."
e:
"Hope" is uncountable (ruling out "few/a few"). "A little" has a positive meaning ("some"), matching "the doctors have not given up".
"Little" (without 'a') has a negative meaning ("hardly any").

q: Choose the correct preposition to complete the sentence: "This vintage edition is far superior _____ the reprinted version."
e:
Latin-derived comparative adjectives ending in "-ior" (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, anterior, posterior) and "preferable" are always followed by "to", never "than".
They also do not take "more" before them (never "more superior").

q: Select the sentence that correctly distinguishes between "elder/eldest" and "older/oldest":
o: He is elder than his cousin by four years.
This is the eldest temple in the entire city.
My elder sister is older than my best friend.
She is the older of my three daughters.
e:
"Elder/eldest" is used exclusively for members of the same family and is never followed by "than" ("elder to" is used if needed).
"Older/oldest" is used for both persons (outside or inside family, with "than") and things (temples, buildings).

q: Fill in the blank accurately: "We cannot proceed without _____ instructions from the principal."
e:
"Further" means "additional" or "more" (abstract/figurative), whereas "farther" refers strictly to greater physical distance ("Delhi is farther from Lucknow than Kanpur").
Here "additional instructions" requires "further".

q: Fill in the blank: "The stern officer made the recruits _____ ten rounds of the parade ground."
e:
Causative verbs like "make" and "let" (in Active Voice), as well as verbs of perception (see, hear, watch), take the BARE INFINITIVE (without "to"): "made the recruits run".
Note: In Passive Voice, "make" takes a full to-infinitive ("The recruits were made to run").

q: Complete the sentence correctly: "I look forward to _____ you at the annual literary conference."
e:
In expressions such as "look forward to", "be used to", "accustomed to", "with a view to", and "addicted to", the word "to" is a PREPOSITION, so it must be followed by a Gerund (-ing form): "meeting".
Using the base verb "meet" after "look forward to" is a classic exam trap.

q: Identify the sentence in which "need" is used correctly as a semi-modal auxiliary verb:
o: He need not worry about the results.
He needs not to worry about the results.
He need not to worry about the results.
Does he need not worry about the results?
e:
As a modal auxiliary in negative/interrogative sentences, "need" takes NO "-s" in third-person singular and is followed by a bare infinitive ("need not worry").
As a regular main verb, it takes "does not need to worry".

q: Fill in the blanks with "very" or "much": "The audience was _____ surprised to see a _____ interesting performance."
e:
"Very" modifies present participles used as adjectives ("very interesting") and positive adjectives, while "much" (or "very much") modifies past participles ("much surprised", "much admired") and comparatives.
Exception: A few past participles like "tired", "pleased", "delighted", and "satisfied" take "very".

q: Choose the sentence that uses "too" accurately in formal standard English:
o: The tea is too hot to drink.
I am too glad to hear of your promotion.
She is too intelligent to win every prize.
He is too healthy to run fast.
e:
"Too" carries a negative excess sense ("more than desirable") and pairs naturally with "to + verb" ("too hot to drink" = so hot that one cannot drink it).
"Too glad" or "too healthy" without a negative result is incorrect; use "very glad" instead.

q: Identify the error in the sentence: "No sooner had the train arrived at the platform (A) / when the passengers rushed (B) / towards the compartments (C) / No error (D)."
o: No sooner had the train arrived at the platform
e:
The correlative conjunction "No sooner" is ALWAYS paired with "than", never with "when" or "then".
Correct form: "No sooner had the train arrived at the platform than the passengers rushed..." ("Hardly/Scarcely" takes "when").

q: Complete the sentence correctly: "Walk carefully on the wet tiles lest you _____."
e:
"Lest" means "for fear that" (already negative), so it is NEVER followed by "not", and it takes the auxiliary "should" (or bare subjunctive): "lest you should slip".
Using "will" or "not" after "lest" is grammatically wrong.

q: Choose the correct article combination: "Kalidasa is often called _____ Shakespeare of India, and he lived in _____ fourth century CE."
e:
When a Proper Noun is used metaphorically as a Common Noun for comparison ("the Shakespeare of India"), it takes "the".
Ordinal numbers ("the fourth century", "the first chapter") also take "the".

q: Which sentence correctly uses or omits the article "the" before institutional nouns (school, hospital, church, prison)?
o: My father went to the hospital to visit his injured colleague.
Every morning, the children go to the school to study.
The wounded soldier was rushed to the hospital for surgery.
The convict was sent to the prison for five years.
e:
Institutional nouns take NO article when visited for their PRIMARY purpose (go to school to study, go to hospital for treatment, go to prison as a convict), but take "the" when visited for a SECONDARY purpose (visiting a colleague at the hospital).
Thus A is correct, whereas B, C, and D incorrectly insert "the".

q: Identify the part of speech of the word "fast" in the two sentences: (1) "Muslims observe a *fast* during Ramadan." (2) "She ran *fast* to catch the bus."
e:
In (1), "a fast" is preceded by the article "a" and acts as the object of "observe", so it is a Noun.
In (2), "fast" modifies the verb "ran" (telling how she ran), so it is an Adverb (note: "fastly" is not a standard English word).

q: Identify the part of speech of the italicized word in: "A *rolling* stone gathers no moss."
e:
"Rolling" qualifies the noun "stone", acting as a verbal adjective—hence a Present Participle.
By contrast, in "Rolling stones down the hill is dangerous," "Rolling" would be a Gerund.

q: Which of the following pairs of singular and plural noun forms shows a DISTINCT CHANGE IN MEANING?
e:
Certain nouns change meaning completely when pluralized: advice (counsel) vs. advices (information/dispatches); good (benefit) vs. goods (merchandise); wood (timber) vs. woods (forest); iron (metal) vs. irons (fetters).
Options B, C, and D merely indicate singular vs. plural number of the same meaning.

q: Spot the sentence that contains NO grammatical error in noun number or verb agreement:
o: The committee are divided in their opinions on the new bill.
Two passer-bys were injured in the accident.
Ten miles are a long distance to walk on foot.
Mathematics are my favourite subject at university.
e:
When a collective noun ("committee") acts as divided individuals, it correctly takes a plural verb ("are") and plural pronoun ("their").
Errors in others: A should be "passers-by"; C should be "Ten miles is..." (single unit of distance); D should be "Mathematics is..." (singular subject name).

q: Choose the formally correct sentence in standard written English:
o: I do not approve of him going to the party alone.
I do not approve of his going to the party alone.
I do not approve of he going to the party alone.
I do not approve of himself going to the party alone.
e:
A noun or pronoun modifying a Gerund ("going") must be in the POSSESSIVE case ("his going", "John's coming"), because the gerund functions as a noun.
Using the objective case "him" is colloquial and considered erroneous in UP TGT formal grammar exams.

q: Spot the error in the sentence: "One must always keep (A) / his promises if one wishes (B) / to earn public trust (C) / No error (D)."
e:
When the indefinite pronoun "one" is the subject, its possessive and reflexive forms MUST remain "one's" and "oneself"—never "his" or "himself".
Correct form: "One must always keep one's promises if one wishes to earn public trust."

q: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT due to the misuse of an absolute (non-gradable) adjective?
o: This is the most unique manuscript in our archive.
Her argument was more persuasive than his.
He is the bravest soldier in the battalion.
The river is narrower here than downstream.
e:
Absolute adjectives such as "unique", "perfect", "universal", "eternal", "round", "ideal", and "chief" already denote the highest or absolute degree and should NOT take "more" or "most".
Correct form: "This is a unique manuscript in our archive."

q: Choose the sentence with the correct standard order of multiple adjectives before a noun:
o: She bought a wooden round antique brown table.
She bought a lovely small antique round brown wooden table.
She bought an antique lovely wooden small brown round table.
She bought a brown wooden lovely small antique round table.
e:
English follows the OSASCOMP adjective order: Opinion (lovely) → Size (small) → Age (antique) → Shape (round) → Colour (brown) → Origin → Material (wooden) → Purpose + Noun (table).
Only Option B follows this exact sequence.

q: Identify the sentence that is FREE from a dangling (misrelated) participle error:
o: Walking through the dense park, a poisonous snake bit him.
Being a rainy day, we decided to stay indoors.
Having finished her homework, Meera went out to play.
Driving down the highway, the tall mountains came into view.
e:
In C, the subject of the main clause ("Meera") is also the logical doer of the participle phrase ("Having finished her homework").
In A, the snake wasn't walking; in B, "we" aren't a rainy day (needs "It being a rainy day"); in D, the mountains weren't driving.

q: Fill in the blank using the formal present subjunctive mood: "The judge ordered that the witness _____ present in court at 10 AM sharp."
e:
After verbs/adjectives of demand, order, or recommendation (order, insist, demand, suggest, recommend, essential + that), formal English uses the bare base verb (Present Subjunctive): "that the witness be present".
It remains "be" regardless of whether the subject is singular or the main verb is past tense.

q: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the past tense of the intransitive verb "lie" (to recline/rest):
o: Exhausted after the trek, he laid down on the cot for an hour.
Exhausted after the trek, he lay down on the cot for an hour.
Exhausted after the trek, he lied down on the cot for an hour.
Exhausted after the trek, he has laid down on the cot for an hour.
e:
Principal parts of the three confusing verbs: (1) Lie–lay–lain (intransitive: recline); (2) Lay–laid–laid (transitive: put/place something); (3) Lie–lied–lied (tell an untruth).
Since "recline" takes no object here, its past tense is "lay".

q: Select the grammatically CORRECT sentence employing negative adverbial inversion:
o: Seldom I have witnessed such extraordinary courage.
Seldom have I witnessed such extraordinary courage.
Hardly he had reached the station when the train left.
Never she spoke a harsh word to anyone.
e:
When a negative or restrictive adverb (Seldom, Never, Hardly, Scarcely, Rarely, Little, Not only) begins a sentence, Subject–Auxiliary Inversion is mandatory: Adverb + Auxiliary + Subject + Main Verb ("Seldom have I witnessed...").
Options A, C, and D omit inversion.

q: Which of the following sentences observes strict grammatical parallelism with "not only...but also"?
o: She not only excels in poetry but also in drama.
She excels not only in poetry but also in drama.
Not only she excels in poetry but also in drama.
She excels in not only poetry but also writes drama.
e:
Correlative conjunctions ("not only...but also", "either...or", "neither...nor") must join grammatically parallel structures.
In B, both elements are parallel prepositional phrases ("in poetry" and "in drama") placed after "excels".

q: Read the sentence carefully: "The Principal and Secretary _____ arrived for the convocation." Which verb is correct, and how many individuals does the subject denote?
o: has — one single individual holding both offices
were — one single individual holding both offices
e:
When two singular nouns joined by "and" share a SINGLE article ("The Principal and Secretary"), they refer to ONE person holding both posts and take a singular verb ("has").
If the article is repeated ("The Principal and the Secretary"), it denotes TWO persons and takes "have".

q: Fill in the blanks accurately: "_____ higher you climb, _____ colder it gets."
e:
In parallel comparative clauses expressing proportional increase or decrease ("the + comparative..., the + comparative..."), the definite article "the" (functioning historically as an adverbial instrumental) is mandatory in both clauses.
Example: "The more you read, the wiser you become."

q: Identify the part of speech of the word "but" in the sentence: "There was none *but* wept at the tragic sight."
e:
After a negative antecedent ("none", "no one"), "but" acts as a Negative Relative Pronoun meaning "who did not" ("There was none who did not weep").
Compare: "All but him" (Preposition = except), "She is but a child" (Adverb = only), "He tried but failed" (Conjunction).

q: Which of the following sentences is grammatically CORRECT regarding the omission of articles?
o: They elected him the chairman of the board.
They elected him chairman of the board.
He was appointed as a director of the institute.
We made him the captain of our school team.
e:
Verbs of appointing, electing, making, or crowning (elect, appoint, make, nominate, crown) take a complement designating a unique office/rank WITHOUT an article (and without "as"): "They elected him chairman of the board."
Options A, C, and D insert unnecessary articles or "as".
